From Middle English affect, from Latin affectus, adfectus (“a state of mind or body produced by some (external) influence, especially sympathy or love”), from afficere (“to act upon, influence”).

senses.d: To influence or alter.
ex: The experience affected me deeply.
The heat of the sunlight affected the speed of the chemical reaction.

senses.d: To move to emotion.
ex: He was deeply affected by the tragic ending of the play.
A consideration of the rationale of our passions seems to me very necessary for all who would affect them upon solid and pure principles.

senses.d: Of an illness or condition, to infect or harm (a part of the body).
ex: Hepatitis affects the liver.

senses.d: To dispose or incline.
ex: men whom they thought best affected to religion and their country's liberty

senses.d: To tend to by affinity or disposition.
ex: The drops of every fluid affect a round figure.

senses.d: To assign; to appoint.
ex: One of the domestics was affected to his special service.

senses.d: To burden (property) with a fixed charge or payment, or other condition or restriction.
To feign or pretend.
ex: The light above the door made it unconvincing to affect that no one was at home.

senses.d: To make a show of; to put on a pretense of; to feign; to assume. To make a false display of.
ex: to affect ignorance

senses.d: To aim for, to try to obtain.
ex: For it is believed, that he never was married, affecting and embracing Chastity through the whole course of his Life.

senses.d: To feel affection for (someone); to like, be fond of.

There is a Lady in Verona heere
Whom I affect: but she is nice, and coy,

From that day forth she gan to him affect, / And daily more her favour to augment […]
